summary: This International Biochar Initiative page explains the equipment and processes used to make biochar, from simple campfires and charcoal kilns to modern bio-refineries. It distinguishes pyrolysis from gasification, describes fast and slow pyrolysis, and surveys farm-scale, small-scale, and continuous-feed production units. It closes with advanced production goals from Robert Brown and a summary of Washington State biochar reports. Website navigation, cookie banners and footers are ignored.
one_line: Overview of biochar production technologies, covering pyrolysis and gasification systems, kilns, ovens, and advanced reactors.
key_facts: Equipment for making biochar can be as simple as a primitive campfire or as complex as a modern bio-refinery, and the basic process is called pyrolysis.
Pyrolysis is the breaking down (lysis) of a material by heat (pyro), and as material breaks down it releases gas.
Pyrolysis systems use kilns and retorts to contain the baking biomass while excluding oxygen, and the gases released are often called "syngas".
Fast pyrolysis tends to produce more oils and liquids, while slow pyrolysis produces more syngas.
Gasification systems produce smaller quantities of biochar in a directly-heated reaction vessel with introduced air.
Biochar production is optimized in the absence of oxygen; the more oxygen a production unit can exclude, the more biochar it can produce.
At the local or regional level, pyrolysis and gasification units can process up to 4,000 kg of biomass per hour.
Small scale gasification and pyrolysis systems for farms or small industries are commercially available with biomass inputs of 50 kg/hr to 1,000 kg/hr.
Biochar ovens have feedstock chambers usually in the range of very small to 4-500 liters.

Since 2007, the Washington Department of Ecology and the Center for Sustaining Agriculture and Natural Resources (CSANR) at Washington State University have produced in-depth reports on biochar production, use, and economics.
The Washington interest in biochar grew out of a state solid waste management plan called Beyond Waste, which created the Organic Waste to Resources project.
The Organic Waste to Resources project was charged with examining ways to use nearly 17 million tons of organic waste identified in Washington State.
Dr. Robert Brown of Iowa State University, Ames, wrote Chapter 8, Biochar Production Technology, of Biochar for Environmental Management.
Advanced goals listed by Dr. Brown include continuous feed pyrolyzers to improve energy efficiency and reduce pollution emissions associated with batch kilns.
